Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording: Fireflies auto transcribe

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Tideway is evaluating Redwood as the inference backend for their conversational product. Key concerns: latency and cost trade-offs, integration with existing LangChain/LlamaIndex stacks, where the gateway/proxy sits in their infra, rate limiting and quotas per tenant, and security requirements (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS). Redwood AE (Jordan) + SE (Marta) walked through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, SDKs, observability hooks and proposed a pilot/bench next week.

Topics: SDKs, LangChain adapters, LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy placement, VPC/Private deployment, Dedicated capacity, rate limits/quotas, observability/tracing hooks, security/KMS, pilot benchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time — I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this deal. With me are Marta and Devon from solutions. How are you all?
[00:08] Evan: Doing good, Jordan. Thanks. We're excited to see how Redwood could replace our current hosted endpoints for the conversational service.
[00:12] Maya: Yeah hi, Maya here. We're mostly focused on integration complexity and how this will sit with our LangChain pipelines.
[00:18] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda — we want to understand Tideway's stack, traffic profile, security must-haves, then show how SDKs + gateway options look, and align on a POC. Marta, can you kick off with the SDK/adapter overview?
[00:28] Marta: Sure. So Redwood has lightweight SDKs — HTTP + native SDKs for Node and Python. For LangChain people we have a connector that maps the Redwood Chat API onto LangChain's LLM/Chat wrappers; similarly we provide a compatibility layer for LlamaIndex connectors so you can swap in Redwood as the model call without reworking retrievers.
[00:44] Marta: There's also streaming support and function/tool calling, and we expose hooks for token-level billing in telemetry. In practice, you install our SDK and either point it at the hosted endpoint, a Dedicated pool endpoint, or a Private VPC endpoint.
[00:59] Maya: So for LangChain, do we change prompts or is it exactly the same interface?
[01:03] Marta: It's minimal — basically you provide a Redwood client, the rest is a thin adapter. There's a small shim for message formats — sometimes role names differ — so we've seen one or two places where you need to normalize. But no heavy refactor.
[01:15] Rohit: How about LlamaIndex? We use LlamaIndex to build context windows and retrieval. Any issues with prefix/KV cache?
[01:21] Marta: Good question. Our runtime supports prefix caching and KV-cache reuse. LlamaIndex usually handles indexing + retriever; you route the final LLM call through Redwood. We do automatic KV caching for repeated prefixes but you may need to adjust your retrieval window size and chunking to get optimal latency.
[01:35] Evan: On latency — our SLAs are pretty strict for user-facing chat (p95 < 250ms). Can you meet that?
[01:40] Marta: p95 < 250ms is tight for long generations. For short responses (<= 64 tokens) Redwood Hosted on the smallest low-latency profile can approach that for small models, but if you want guaranteed throughput and lower p95, Dedicated with pinned GPU pools and tuned batching is the path. We can also do model variants — quantized c-api types or trimmed context models — to reduce tail latency. There's some tradeoff with cost and quality.
[02:00] Maya: If we go Dedicated, what's the minimum commit and how does burst capacity work?
[02:05] Jordan: Dedicated is a reserved capacity product — minimum is typically a monthly commit depending on region. We also offer burst capacity buckets for spikes; those are billed per-minute or token-based depending on configuration. I'll share the pricing tiers after the call.
[02:20] Rohit: Architecturally we want to put a gateway/proxy in front of the models because we have multi-tenant routing and custom rate limits per account. Does Redwood work behind a gateway?
[02:29] Devon: Absolutely. Many customers run an edge gateway that handles tenancy, authentication, and per-tenant quotas, then proxy to Redwood. You can also use Redwood's routing policies to gate by tenant — e.g., route premium tenants to Dedicated and rest to Hosted. If you prefer, we provide a small on-prem proxy connector that speaks gRPC/HTTP and authenticates to our control plane.
[02:47] Lena: From a security perspective, we need SSO (SAML), RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration for key material. Also data residency constraints for EU customers.
[02:58] Marta: We integrate with major SSO providers via SAML/OIDC and offer RBAC in the Console. We produce audit logs with request-level metadata; for Private deployments you can keep logs in your VPC. KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private and can be configured for Dedicated as well with customer-managed keys — though Hosted will use Redwood-managed keys unless you opt for an enterprise KMS pairing.
[03:19] Evan: Does Private allow air-gapped on-prem? We have a couple of regulated clients asking for that on certain workloads.
[03:23] Marta: Yes — Private includes VPC-hosted control plane and an on-prem package for air-gapped installs, though that requires an enterprise engagement. We can provide the architecture doc and the checklist.
[03:33] Maya: Observability — what telemetry do you expose? We need traces across our gateway into the inference call to correlate latency and token cost.
[03:40] Devon: We emit per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns. There's a tracing hook that you can attach to your existing APM (Zipkin/Jaeger/DataDog), and we also export per-model, per-route dashboards in the Redwood Console. You can set retention windows and tag traces by tenant id.
[03:58] Rohit: Rate limiting — can Redwood enforce per-customer quotas or do we have to enforce that at the gateway?
[04:04] Marta: You can do either. Many customers prefer the gateway for throttling and to shape traffic pre-inference. Redwood has built-in rate limiters and quota policies at the API key/token level; these can be configured per-customer if you create sub-keys or route tokens. We'll show a policy example in the POC.
[04:18] Evan: We use LangChain + LlamaIndex heavily; any gotchas around streaming responses and retrievers?
[04:24] Marta: Streaming works fine with LangChain's streaming callbacks, but keep an eye on backpressure in your retriever loops. If your retriever returns large contexts, that increases generation time and token cost. Consider summarizing or using a shorter window for user-visible chats.
[04:38] Maya: How do you handle function calling / structured outputs? We rely on structured JSON responses from the model for downstream orchestration.
[04:45] Marta: Redwood supports function calling semantics and structured outputs. We return the function call as part of the streamed payload and also provide a compact structured-response endpoint if you want stricter schema enforcement. There's also support for response validation hooks in the SDK.
[04:59] Lena: A few compliance questions — do you have SOC2 type II and do you provide exportable audit logs for compliance reviews?
[05:05] Jordan: Yes, we are SOC2 Type II — we'll share the attestation and the standard security pack. Audit logs are exportable; for Private deployments logs can stay in-customer storage.
[05:15] Evan: For the POC, we want to run a 72-hour simulated load with a traffic generator to measure p95, token cost, and failover. Can Redwood support that?
[05:23] Marta: Yes. For benchmarking we can deploy a Dedicated pilot or use Hosted with synthetic traffic. If you need consistent results, Dedicated with pinned GPUs is best, but we can also run a controlled hosted bench and instrument the traces so you get token-level cost. We'll need a sample dataset and traffic profile.
[05:37] Rohit: Any rate-limiting impacts during bench? We don't want the Redwood rate limits to throttle our synthetic traffic and skew the numbers.
[05:43] Devon: For the bench we'll provision a test key with elevated quotas or route to a Dedicated test pool so there are no noisy neighbors. We'll also capture metrics and share dashboards.
[05:54] Maya: On the SDK side, how invasive is the change? We have some microservices in Go and our orchestration layer is Python.
[06:00] Marta: We have a Go SDK alpha and a mature Python SDK. For multi-language setups you can keep the gateway as the single LLM client and have services call it. That centralizes quotas and simplifies observability.
[06:11] Evan: A quick question on billing: is it per-token for hosted, and for Dedicated is it a flat commit + token overage?
[06:18] Jordan: Hosted is per-token + request unit rates for embeddings/generation. Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commit; we offer overage pricing and token reporting. We'll put the exact numbers in the pricing sheet.
[06:27] Lena: Will customer data be used to improve Redwood models? This is a hard stop for some of our clients.
[06:33] Marta: By default Hosted may retain data for service quality but enterprise contracts can opt-out. For Dedicated/Private, data is isolated and not used to train or fine-tune public models; we'll sign appropriate DPA/terms.
[06:44] Rohit: Are there any known integration issues with LlamaIndex when using large context windows + streaming?
[06:50] Marta: The main practical issue is chunk size and request concurrency. If you simultaneously stream and stream multiple retrievals, you could see higher tails due to disk I/O or KV cache misses. Our recommendation is to tune retrieval concurrency and enable prefix caching for repeated system messages.
[07:07] Evan: For the pilot, can you run a config with quantized models? We want to see quality vs cost.
[07:12] Marta: Yes — we can run q4f/q8 variants in the bench. Quality regressions are evaluated against your prompt set; we can run side-by-side evals and produce BLEU-like/embedding-sim scores.
[07:25] Maya: Observability hooks — can we ingest Redwood logs into our ELK stack?
[07:30] Devon: Yes — we export JSON logs and metrics to S3/Kafka/HTTP endpoints and have direct integrations for Datadog, Splunk, and ELK. You can stream audit logs to your retention store.
[07:41] Evan: Great. Let's talk timeline — we want a POC next week and then a decision by end of month if numbers look good.
[07:49] Jordan: Sounds doable. Proposed next steps: Marta runs bench, Jordan sends pricing/security docs, and we reconvene after bench with results.
[07:57] Rohit: One more thing — our gateway currently uses a signed JWT per-tenant. Can Redwood accept signed tokens or do you need API keys?
[08:03] Marta: We can accept signed JWTs at the gateway level — many customers do that and exchange them for short-lived Redwood tokens. If you want us to validate JWT claims we can configure that in the proxy.
[08:14] Lena: How do you handle model rollouts / canary? We have different tenants and want safe rollouts.
[08:19] Devon: Redwood supports canary rollouts and routing policies by tenant tag. You can route a percentage of traffic to a new model variant and have automatic fallback policies if quality/latency degrades.
[08:30] Maya: Ok good. Any blockers we haven't covered?
[08:34] Evan: The only blockers are a clear cost model, security docs, and a bench run.
[08:38] Jordan: We'll cover those. Marta, can you confirm bench requirements after — like dataset size, tokens per request distribution, concurrency?
[08:46] Marta: Yes, we'll follow up. Please share a small sample of the convo logs (PII scrubbed) and a desired SLA profile. Also share the list of tenants we want to simulate and per-tenant quotas.
[08:59] Maya: We'll prepare that today.
[09:02] Jordan: Alright — quick recap before we close. Next steps: 1) Jordan to email pricing + Dedicated options and pilot terms by 2026-03-24. 2) Marta to run bench and share dashboards by 2026-03-29. 3) Tideway to share sample prompts & traffic profile by EOD 2026-03-22. 4) Schedule POC kickoff with Tideway infra (Jordan to propose times). Any additions?
[09:22] Evan: That covers it. Thanks everyone.
[09:25] Lena: Thanks. We'll loop legal in once we get the security pack.
[09:29] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up.
